content: Incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) is a prevalent skin condition in adults who experience urinary, fecal, or dual incontinence. The same products and procedures are typically used for both the prevention and treatment of IAD. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various products and procedures in preventing and treating IAD in adults. The researchers conducted an extensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, CINAHL, and others, up to September 28, 2016. They also reviewed conference proceedings, reference lists of relevant articles, and consulted experts in the field. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving participants aged 18 years or older, with or without IAD, in any healthcare setting. The trials compared the (cost) effectiveness of topical skin care products, such as cleansers, moisturizers, and skin protectants, as well as skin care procedures designed to prevent and treat IAD. Thirteen trials involving 1,316 participants were included in the qualitative synthesis. The participants were incontinent for urine, stool, or both, and were either nursing home residents or hospitalized patients. Most trials had small sample sizes and short follow-up periods, and the overall risk of bias was high. Due to significant variability in participant populations, products, procedures, outcomes, and measurement tools, the data were unsuitable for meta-analysis. Nine trials compared different topical skin care products, including combinations of products. Two trials evaluated structured skin care procedures. One trial compared topical skin care products with varying frequencies of application, while another trial focused solely on the frequency of application of these products. Two trials provided evidence, albeit of low to moderate quality, that soap and water were less effective in preventing and treating IAD. The first trial suggested that using a skin cleanser was more effective than soap and water, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.39 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.17 to 0.87; low-quality evidence). The second trial indicated that a structured skin care procedure, involving a washcloth with cleansing, moisturizing, and protective properties, was more effective than soap and water, with an RR of 0.31 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.79; moderate-quality evidence). Other trials, all of low to very low quality, suggested that applying leave-on products, such as moisturizers, skin protectants, or combinations of these, might be more effective than not using such products. However, no trial reported on the third primary outcome, which was the number of participants dissatisfied with treatment, nor did they report on adverse effects. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence, ranging from very low to moderate quality, regarding the effectiveness of interventions for preventing and treating IAD in adults. Soap and water were found to perform poorly in both prevention and treatment. The application of leave-on products, such as moisturizers and skin protectants, and avoiding soap appear to be more effective. The effectiveness of leave-on products depends on their ingredients, formulation, and usage, such as the amount applied. The authors emphasized the need for high-quality, confirmatory trials using standardized and comparable prevention and treatment regimens across different settings and regions. They also recommended the development of a core outcome set, including validated measurement tools, to improve the comparability of trial results. The evidence in this review is current as of September 28, 2016.
